lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Senior Advocate (M Nurullah, Senior Advocate and Mahmudul Islam, Advocate with him) instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-an-Record ------- For the Appellant.

AW Bhuiyan, Additional Attorney-General (B Hossain, Deputy Attorney- General and Sharifuddin Chaklader, Assistant Attorney-General with him) instructed by A W Mallik, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Respondents.
parties:
National Engineers Ltd ------- Appellant.
Vs.
Director, Military Lands and Cantonment Directorate, Ministry of Defence, Dhaka Cantonment and others ------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J. : The appellant, a Private Limited Company incorporated in Bangladesh under the Companies Act, 1913, is in possession of an industrial unit, namely, a drum manufacturing factory formerly, belonging to MIs Drums Metal Ltd., located at Airport Road, Tejgaon, Dhaka on a leasehold land of 3.28 acres, in pursuance of an agreement for sale dated 13.9.77 entered into between the appellant and the President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. The appellant received a Notice dated 15.6.88 from respondent No. 1, Director, Military Lands and Cantonments Directorate, Ministry of Defence (Annexure 'A' to the writ petition) stating that the lease of the land had expired on 31.3.86 and that it had not been renewed and directing the appellant to remove by 22.6.88 all the goods and machineries of the drums factory from the leasehold land for handing over the same to the Works Ministry. By a further Notice dated 18.6.88 (Annexure 'B' to the Writ Petition) issued under section 3 of the Central Government Lands and Buildings (Recovery of Possession) Ordinance, 1965, shortly the Ordinance, respondent No.2, the Administrator of Military Lands, Military Land Administration Directorate, Central Circle, Dhaka Cantonment stated that 2.26 acres of land had already been resumed and directed the appellant to vacate the remaining 1.02 acres of land within 22.6.88 failing which action would be taken under sections 6 and 7 of the Ordinance. The appellant challenged these two notices dated 15.6.88 and 18.6.88 (Annexures 'A' and 'B') in Writ Petition No. 1215 of 1988 as having been issued without any lawful authority and to be of no legal effect and calling for a direction upon the respondents to cancel, rescind or withdraw the same. By judgment and order dated 27.8.91 the High Court Division discharged the Rule. This appeal is by leave from the said judgment and order. 

 4. The disputed land measuring 3.28 acres admittedly belongs to the Government and is managed by the Ministry of Defence as military land (being inside the cantonment area). The lease in respect of the said land, according to the respondents, had expired on 31.3.86 and the appellant's occupation thereof had therefore become unauthorised. The appellant, on the other hand, contends that it is possessing the land on the basis of an agreement for sale dated 13.9.77 (Annexure 'D') entered into between it and the Government in the Ministry of Industries, that it had a bona fide claim of right to possess the land, that it is neither a lessee under the Government (in the Ministry of Defence) nor an unauthorised occupant as alleged, and as such the Ordinance for recovery of possession of the disputed land was not attracted and the notices were thus illegal and without lawful authority. 

 7. The learned Additional Attorney-General has produced papers to show that an area of 61.97 acres of land of a number of CS plots, including the disputed CS plot Nos. 34 and 42 of mouza Tejkunipara, PS Tejgaon, District Dhaka was acquired by the Central Government of India under Rule 75A(2) of the Defence of India Rules, by a Notification dated 10.7.46 published in the Calcutta Gazette on 17.10.46. M/s Allenberry &Co. established a factory for manufacture of drums on 12.50 acres of the aforesaid acquired land, including the disputed land of 3.28 acres. The Central Government sanctioned on 27.11.59 the grant of a lease of 12.50 acres of land to M/s Allenberry &Co for a period of 30 years with effect from 1.4.53. 

 8. The disputed land belongs to the Government in a cantonment and therefore it is a Military Land, managed and administered by the Ministry of Defence, as per Rules of Business, 1975. In exercise of powers under section 280 of the Cantonments Act, 1924 the Central Government framed the Cantonment Land Administration Rules, 1937, shortly the Rules, Rule 4 of which classifies land in Cantonments into three categories-(l) Land which "is vested in His Majesty". (Classes A and B); (2) Land which "is vested in the Cantonment Board" (Class C) and (3) Land which falls into neither of the first two categories. The disputed land falls into Class B( 4) in the first category. General Land Register shows that the disputed land has been classified as Class B(4) land. The Military Estates Officers appointed under Rule 2(e) are the agents of the Government for the administration of Class B(4) category of land. They hold a position of official independence from the Military authorities and are also officially independent of the Cantonment Boards and are subject to the orders of the Central Government alone (Vide Government of India Notification No. 34724/l/AD dated 12.8.27). Rule 15 provides that the sale of land for any purpose without the definite orders of the Central Government is prohibited. Rule 31(1) also provides that a lease for a building site for a period not exceeding 30 years or a lease in perpetuity may be granted by the Military Estates Officer in the forms described in Schedules IX and X. No such lease shall be granted without previous consultation with the Collector and the previous sanction of the Central Government. 

 10. M/s Drums Metal Ltd. took over the drum factory from Mis Allenberry &Co. and a fresh sanction was given by the Government of Pakistan, Ministry of Defence of 3.5.69 amending the lease in favour of M/s Drums Metal Ltd. and reducing the area from 12.50 acres to 7.93 acres for a period of 20 years with effect from 1.4.63 (Annexure-2 to the Affidavit-in-Opposition of respondent Nos. 1 and 2). 

 11. M/s Drums Metal Ltd. was a company consisting of Pakistani share-holders and after liberation its aforesaid industrial undertaking at Tejgaon became an abandoned property under the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 (PO No. 16 of 1972), Article 4 of which provided that "on the commencement of this Order, all abandoned properties in Bangladesh shall vest in the Government and shall be administered, controlled, managed and disposed of, by transfer or otherwise, in accordance with the provisions of this Order". As M/s Drums Metal Ltd. was an industrial undertaking, its control, management and disposal was placed under the Ministry of Industries as per Rule 6 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Taking over Possession) Rules, 1972. The said Ministry in turn entrusted the administration thereof to Bangladesh Steel & Engineering Corporation. 

 12. The Government decided to disinvest, inter alia, the said industrial unit and accordingly published a public notice on 21.4.76 which caused a flutter in the Ministry of Defence which by a letter dated 12.5.76 requested the Ministry of Industries not to take any steps in respect of Military Lands leased out to M/s Drums Metal Ltd. 

 16. The price quoted by the appellant for 7.93 acres was Tk. 91,00,000'00, but for the reduced area of 3.28 acres the Ministry of Industries asked for the same amount and the appellant agreed after failing in its attempt to secure a proportionate reduction in the price. A letter of intent dated 7.6.77 was issued by respondent No: 3 which was accepted by the appellant which made a down payment of Tk. 22,00,000'00 to the Government as required by the letter of intent. 

 20. The appellant took possession of the lands measuring 3.28 acres and all the undertakings of MIs Drums Metal Ltd. on 13.9.77 after the execution of the agreement for sale. The appellant has thereafter paid Tk. 82,08,521'00 to the Government by way of yearly installment and as to the balance amount of Tk. 8,91,479'00 with interest, the appellant wrote to the Ministry of Industries on 18.9.86 expressing its readiness to pay the same on hearing that the Ministry of Industries was ready and able to execute the sale-deed. The appellant has also been paying every year Tk. 1771'53 to the Military Estates Officer towards annual rent and it has paid a further amount totalling Tk. 60,00,000'00 including interest to Agrani Bank. The appellant asserts that it has spent a huge amount of Tk. 6.5 crores for repair and renovation of the machineries and equipments of the factory by taking loan from Commercial Banks mortgaging personal properties and assets of the Directors of the appellant-Company. The appellant asserted in the writ petition that it had acquired an indefeasible right, title and interest in the drum factory and the lands underneath. 

 "In this context it is mentioned that title over the enterprise is still with the Government and the buyers have been given only the possessory right till the final payment, as per deed of agreement for sale, is made, the Government has huge stake in the enterprise in the form of realisation of sales price. The enterprise is the only unit in the country in the drum manufacturing sector and nature of the machinery and their installations are such that their removal and shifting are likely to result in their being damaged. Moreover, a contractual obligation as per agreement for sale on the part of the Government is there and the apprehension of buyer's suing the Government in Court and the Government, being ordered to pay huge compensation to the buyers cannot be ruled out." 

 24. The Ministry of Industries proposed an Inter-ministerial meeting but nothing ensued from it. The Military Estates Officer initiated a Certificate Proceeding against the appellant under the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 for rea1isation of the premium and rent as demanded by him by his letter dated 9.3.86. The appellant filed an objection and the Certificate Officer after hearing the parties by his order dated 20.9.87 dismissed the case holding that the claim was not realisable under the said Act. 

 26. On these facts it was contended by the appellant before the High Court Division that the appellant was neither a lessee nor an inductee of the lessee nor an unauthorised occupant but. is in possession of the disputed land on the strength of the agreement Annexure 'D' and that its legal right to continue to possess the disputed land cannot be invaded by the impugned notices issued under the Ordinance. The High Court Division paid no notice to this submission. It was also contended that on the representation of the Government through the Ministry of Industries, respondent No.3, the appellant had acquired an indefeasible right to use and occupy the disputed land. The theory of promissory estoppel was invoked and a massive argument and counter-argument was advanced by both sides on the theory of promissory estoppel, which commanded the entire attention of the High Court Division. It rejected the plea of promissory estoppel and held that respondent No.3 did not give any assurance or promise that there would be a sale of the land. It also held that on the expiry of the period of leasehold interest the appellant was not only an unauthorised occupant of the disputed land but had also no legal right to maintain the writ petition. 

 27. Before this Court Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Counsel for the appellant, has given up a number of positions taken up by the appellant in the High Court Division. No longer contending that the appellant was unaware of the leasehold nature of the disputed land before the agreement for sale, and that the appellant was entitled to an absolute ownership of the disputed land, he now contends that the appellant knew about the leasehold character of the disputed land, but it had a reasonable expectation that an extension of lease for a further reasonable period would be a mere formality and a routine affair. He has also given up the highly contentious claim of promissory estoppel which the High Court Division rejected. In fact leave was granted to consider (1) whether the High Court Division wrongly did not answer the moot question whether the appellant's possession of the disputed land under an agreement for sale with the Government can be said to be the possession of a lessee or a person inducted by the lessee so as to attract the mischief of the Ordinance and whether, if the Ordinance applies, the appellant's possession can be said to be one under a bona fide claim of right, (2) whether the High Court Division was right in holding that the appellant was an unauthorised occupant of the disputed land and (3) whether it was rightly held that the appellant had no legal right and therefore the writ petition was not maintainable. 

 "3. If, on the expiry, whether before or after the commencement of this Ordinance, of the period of any lease or licence in respect of any land or building of which the Central Government is the lessor or llicencee or on the determination of such lease or licence on the ground of breach of any covenant imposing an obligation on the lessee or licencee to give up possession of the demised land or building required for any public purpose, the lessee or licencee refused or failed, or refuses or fails, to vacate that land or building and puts the Central Government into possession of the same, any officer authorized by the Central Government in this behalf may, notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, at any time, enter upon the demised land or building and recover vacant possession of that land or building by evicting the lessee or licencee and may also demolish and remove the structures, if any, erected of built thereon by the lessee or licencee: 

 "2(e). "unauthorized occupant" means a person who is in occupation of any land or building without the express permission or authority of the Central Government, and includes- 

 31. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed submits that the Ordinance does not apply to the appellant, for it is not a lessee within the meaning of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. No document of lease has been executed between the Government and the appellant. But from the fact of the appellant's payment of rent since 13.9.77 and also from the fact that an extension of lease from 31.3.83 to 31.3.86 was sanctioned by the Ministry of Defence in favour of the appellant, the learned Additional Attorney-General sought to argue that the appellant was a lessee and was squarely within the ambit of the Ordinance. We do not think so. The relationship between the lessor and lessee-is a jural relationship, cautiously guarded by section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act. We do not find any material to describe the appellant as a lessee of the disputed land within the initial meaning of the said Act. 

 32. Mr. Ahmed next submits that the appellant is also not a person inducted by the lessee into the disputed land, within the extended meaning of the term "lessee" under section 2(c) of the Ordinance, because the disputed land being a Government land and the leasehold interest having vested in the Government under Article 4 of PO No. 16 of 1972 there is a merger of the leasehold interest in the lessor. Consequently, according to him, the lease is extinguished and the Government cannot be a lessor and a lessee of the same land at the same time. The Government did not act as a lessee while inducting the appellant in the disputed land. If it be held that the Government so acted, then amounts to saying that the Government is evicting itself. Such actions are against good government and public policy, he submits. 

 The plain fact is that the interest of MIs Drums Metal Ltd. as lessee and the interest of the Government in the Ministry of Defence as lessor have not vested in the Government in the Ministry of Industries "in the same right". For, the Government in the Ministry of Industries acting under PO No. 16 of 1972 cannot deal with the disputed land as a lessor, because of the constraints of vesting contained in PO No. 16 of 1972 itself. PO No. 16 of 1972 is about vesting in the Government of abandoned property and the word "property" is defined in Article 2(v) thereof in the following manner:- 

 34. The "right" or "interest" that M/s Drums Metal Ltd. had in the disputed land was that of a lessee and only that right or interest had vested in the Government under PO No. 16 of 1972. The vesting does not go beyond that. A statutory vesting cannot go beyond the terms of the statute itself. The Government acting in the Ministry of Industries under PO No. 16 of 1972 could not have assumed either the paramount ownership of or the lessor's interest in the disputed land. It could only have acquired that interest which MIs Drums Metal Ltd. itself had, nothing more, nothing less. If M/s Drums Metal Ltd. could have sold only the remainder of the leasehold interest in the disputed land, so could the Government acting under PO No. 16 of 1972. The question of merger does not arise. It is not material whether before the agreement for sale the appellant knew about this legal position or not, so long as there was no misrepresentation on facts on the part of respondent No.3. We find there was none. 

 35. It is unnecessary, in our opinion, to enter into a legal polemics as to who was the 'lessee' of the disputed land when the appellant was inducted therein. The plain fact is that the leasehold interest of MIs Drums Metal Ltd. vested in the Government. Article 4 of PO No. 16 of 1972 gives the Government the power to administer, control, manage and dispose of, by transfer or otherwise, the said leasehold interest 

 "5(1) For the purpose of carrying the provisions of PO No. 16 of 1972 into effect, and in particular for the purpose of securing, administration, control, management and disposal, by transfer or otherwise, of abandoned property, the Government may take such measures as it considers necessary or expedient and do all acts and incur all expenses necessary or incidental thereto." 

 Thus the entire bundle of rights and liabilities that MIs Drums Metal Ltd. had in the disputed land now vests in the Government and the Government is statutorily armed to do all that MIs Drums Metal Ltd. itself could do in assertion of its rights and in discharge of its liabilities in respect of the leasehold land. The act of inducting the appellant in the disputed land in part performance of an agreement for sale is an exercise of the Government's power under Articles 4 and 5 of PO No. 16 of 1972. Articles 4 and 5 give the Government the lessee's rights and powers and whatever it does in exercise of that power is a statutory exercise of the lessee's powers. Any action taken by the Government in connection with the disposal of the leasehold interest by transfer, which necessarily included agreement to transfer, will be taken to be a statutorily permissible act and will also be taken to be the act of the lessee. The appellant's induction into the disputed land was made not by the lessee itself, but by a statutorily authorised Ministry of the Government, which had the necessary legal sanction to perform all the acts of the lessee. Therefore, the induction of the appellant in the disputed land by the Government was as if by the lessee itself which became unable or disabled to do anything rendering the disputed property abandoned under PO No. 16 of 1972. 

 39. The Ordinance empowers the Government to issue a notice under section 5 of the Ordinance upon an "unauthorised occupant" of any land or building to vacate the same. Since no notice was issued by the respondents under section 5 of the Ordinance, the High Court Division unnecessarily found the appellant to be an "unauthorized occupant" of the disputed land. In fact, we do not find it necessary to decide whether the appellant was an 'unauthorized occupant", since the notice served upon him was under section 3 of the Ordinance. We have already held that the appellant falls within the mischief of section 3. 

 41. From a history of this case it is quite clear that the dichotomy between the Government in the Ministry of Defence and the Government in the Ministry of Industries, as representing the lessor and the leasehold interest respectively, need to be maintained, because of the character of the land and because of the constraints of PO No. 16 of 1972. The appellant had not, as a cautious buyer, inserted any provision in the agreement for sale protecting its own investment, including purchase price, in case the lease is not extended beyond 31.3.83. It thought it would be a routine affair. It depended upon a decision of Disinvestment Board in which the Ministry of Industries agreed to take up the matter of extension before the lease expired on 31.3.83. The appellant was not a party thereto. The Ministry of Industries indeed took up the matter, pleaded for the appellant as effectively as it could, but the lessor in the Ministry of Defence needed the land for a different purpose. The sanctioning authority would not give any extension beyond 31.3.86. There ended the obligation of the Ministry of Industries. It had no legal obligation to obtain for the appellant an extension of lease for any number of years. The various papers relied upon by the appellant are in the nature of exhortations to the lessor by the Ministry of Industries. These exhortations do not give the appellant a bona fide right to possess the disputed land. 

 42. Mr. Ahmed in aid of his submission as to a bona fide right to possess referred to the decisions in Syed Hatem Ali and others, 12 DLR 804 and Sufia Khatun, 20 DLR (SC) 18. In those cases, the petitioners were sought to be evicted by the Government under the East Bengal Government Lands and Buildings (Recovery of Possession) Act 1953 which was similar to the Ordinance. It has been held that if there is a bona fide dispute regarding title to the lands in question the Act will not be applicable. In the first case, the petitioners claimed to be tenants by virtue of settlement from the Zamindars while the Government denied such tenancy. In Supreme Court case it was found on facts that there appeared to be a bona fide dispute concerning title to the land in question between the parties. In the present case, no such question of title is involved because the Government is admittedly the owner of the disputed land. The decisions do not therefore support the proposition of the learned Counsel. This case falls to be decided not on the principle enunciated in those cases but on the basis whether the stipulation in the Agreement for Sale as to possession affords any protection to the appellant to remain on the land. It is admitted by the appellant that under the said Agreement it cannot claim/enforce ownership of the land but it is limited to a leasehold interest only. The term of the lease having come to an end finally on 31.3.86 there remains no basis for the possession of the appellant to continue. The possession becomes unauthorised since that date. Section 3 of the Ordinance, inter alia, says that upon the expiry of the period of any lease any officer may notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract at any time, enter upon the demised land or building and recover vacant possession 	(underlined by me). Thus the Agreement for sale which has been the sheet anchor of the appellant's case is of no avail to it in any view of the matter once the period of lease is over. The appellant has thus no bona fide right whatever to continue in possession. 

 46. The short point involved in this appeal is, whether the appellant who is admittedly in possession of the factory; Drums Metal Limited, on the lease-hold land of the Government of Bangladesh by virtue of an' agreement for sale dated 13.9.77 can be evicted under section 3 of the Central Government Lands and Buildings (Recovery of Possession) Ordinance, 1965, herein briefly called the Ordinance. 

 47. Facts are not at all in dispute in appeal. I need not write in detail the factual aspect of the case as in the judgment of my learned brother Mustafa Kamal, J' details of all facts have been very elaborately delineated. Suffice it to say, that Drums Metal Industries Limited which is a factory for manufacturing of Drums was taken over as an Abandoned Property and the same vested in the Government of Bangladesh under President's Order No 16 of 1972 and was being administered and managed by the Ministry of Industries in accordance with Rules framed there under. The Ministry of Industries in the Government of Bangladesh having decided to disinvest the undertaking of the said Drums Metal Industries Limited as a Government Policy decision made due advertisement and the appellant submitted tender. Ultimately, the Ministry of Industries accepted the offer of the appellant and proposed to sell 3.28 acres of lease-hold land along with the machineries, plants and other structures of Drums Metal Industries Limited. Pursuant to that, agreement for sale was entered into between the President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh as Seller and the appellant as purchaser on 13.9.77 and possession was handed over to the appellant on the same day. 

 49. Ordinance No. LIV of 1965 is meant for speedy recovery of possession of Government lands and buildings. The preamble of this Ordinance makes it clear that the outgoing lessees, licencees and unauthorised occupants can be evicted in a summary mariner by taking recourse to this Ordinance. Section 2 of this Ordinance defines "Lessee" "licencee" and "Unauthorised Occupant", Section 2(c) of the Ordinance speaks that "Lease" and "Lessee" have the same meaning as in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and for the purpose of section 3, "Lessee" includes his heirs, assigns, legal representative and all persons inducted by the lessee into the demise land or building. Section 3 of the Ordinance relates to eviction of outgoing lessees and licencees from lands or building and section 4 relates to revocation of licence and recovery of possession of building in certain cases. 

 50. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Advocate for the appellant, submits that this ordinance has no manner of application in this case, as because the appellant is not a lessee in the land, nor its occupation in the lease-hold land can be said to be unauthorised, as the appellant is admittedly in possession as inducted by the Ministry of Industries in the Government of Bangladesh pursuant to an agreement for sale. 

 51. The Learned Advocate further submits that Ministry of Industries which was selling the factory along with the lease-hold land on behalf of the Government of Bangladesh was really acting as the vested owner of the Drums Metal Industries Ltd. as paramount owner. The learned Advocate for the appellant submits that in the present case the Government of Bangladesh is the owner/lessor of the factory and land and the Government is competent to establish jural relationship between the appellant and the Government. The Government having inducted the appellant as a purchaser the appellant is neither a lessee nor inducted by the lessee. According to him there was no lease document with the appellant. The lease document which is on record is the lease document between the President of Bangladesh as Lessor and Drums Metal Industries Ltd. as lessee dated 15.7.77 and in that lease document the area of the land was shown as 3.28 acres and the lease was to expire on the 31st of March, 1983. That lease was prior to the agreement of the appellant by which the appellant was inducted into possession. Hence, he argues that it will be totally misnomer to say that the appellant is also a lessee or a person inducted by the lessee within section 2(c) of the Ordinance. Even he contends that within the extended meaning of a "Lessee" as defined in section 2(c) of the Ordinance, it cannot be said that the appellant was inducted into the demised land by the lessee. According to the learned Advocate for the appellant, the Ordinance clearly contemplates speedy recovery of possession of the Government land from private individuals who are outgoing lessees, licencees and unauthorised occupants. 

 52. The learned Additional Attorney-General submits, first, that the Drums Metal Industries Ltd. having been vested in the Government of Bangladesh by operation of law, the Government acquired the interest of the lessee and the appellant thereafter having been inducted into possession by the Ministry of Industries in the Government of Bangladesh, the appellant comes within the extended meaning of section 2(c) of the Ordinance as a person inducted by the lessee. 

 53. The second argument of the learned Additional Attorney-General is that, the factory absolutely vests in the Government by operation of law but the lease-hold interest in the land vests in the Ministry of Industries, Government of Bangladesh only up to 31st of March, 1983 and thereafter up to 31st March, 1986 and as such by the agreement the Ministry of Industries could not transfer more than what really vested in the Ministry of Industries in respect of the lease-hold land of the factory. 

 54. Now to understand the nature of transaction and the stand taken by the parties, I am first to consider the main stipulations as embodied in the agreement itself. When the agreement was entered into on 13.9.77, the appellant made a down payment of Taka 22 lacs out of total consideration of 91 lacs and the balance amount of Taka 69 lacs was to be paid in 9 equal installments with effect from 21.6.78 to the credit of the seller. Each of the aforesaid annual installment shall have to be paid by the purchaser on the rust week of each year to be reckoned from the date of aforesaid down payment. Another stipulation was that the appellant was inducted into possession of "Demised property" and would be entitled to hold and continue to possess the same subject to the conditions of this agreement. In the agreement it was further stipulated that the registration of necessary document would be made within 3 months from the date of payment of the last installment i.e. in September, 1986. There was also a default clause in the agreement that in the event of default of any installment the agreement would be terminated within 15 days' notice to the purchaser and the seller would be entitled to take over possession of the "Demised property" without any let or hindrance from the purchaser. In the schedule of the agreement the assets to be sold included the land measuring 3.28 acres. Thus, admittedly on the agreement the appellant got possession of the "Demised property". It further appears that after the Ministry of Industries advertised for sale of the factory, the Ministry of Defence intimated to the Ministry of Industries not to transfer the land without the consent of the Ministry of Defence. Subsequently, a meeting was held between the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Industries on 9.8.76 in which the original lease-hold land of Drums Metal Ltd. which was 7.93 acres was reduced to 3.28 acres and the Ministry of Defence took possession of 4.65 acres of vacant land from the factory premises. The appellant who was a tendered was also informed by the letter dated 19.5.77 that the quantum of land had been reduced to 3.28 acres and the lease of land would expire on 31.3.1983. In the meanwhile, the Disinvestment Board held a meeting on 20.5.77 and the Board took a decision to sell Drums Metal Ltd. along with the lease-hold land and decided that the matter of extension of lease would be taken up between the Ministry of Industries and Ministry of Defence in 1983 which is the year of expiry of the current lease. In such background possession was given to the appellant on 13.9.77 after the execution of the agreement for sale by the Government of Bangladesh. Keeping all these admitted fact in my mind, I am to see whether the appellant can be lawfully evicted by taking recourse to the ordinance in this case. It is not disputed that the land belongs to the Government of Bangladesh and is managed by the Ministry of Defence. 

 56. I must say that in deciding the case, I am primarily concerned with the question of eviction of the appellant from the land. The Ministry of Industries in the Government of Bangladesh has not yet transferred the factory and the land. The Government has only entered into an agreement for sale and have given possession to the appellant. The appellant was relying upon a contract of sale and the equity for defending his possession against the order of eviction made by the respondents taking recourse to the procedure of summary eviction under the Ordinance without avoiding or cancelling the contract entered into between it and the Government. I am not really concerned with the ultimate question of extension of lease in the lease-hold land in this appeal. The possessory right of the appellant is only threatened under the cover of the Ordinance. The appellant is only trying to protect his possessory interest by virtue of the agreement. Whether by the full performance of the agreement, the appellant will not get more than the lease-hold interest which according to the respondents expired on 31.3.83 was not at all a relevant matter in granting relief to the appellant. 

 57.  It appears from the papers filed in this case that, before execution of the agreement for sale and inducting the appellant into possession, the Ministry of Industries kept abreast the appellant regarding all developments of the proposed sale of the factory and even 4 months prior to the agreement the Disinvestment Board took the decision that the question of extension of lease-hold right in the land would be taken at the time of expiry of the lease in 1983. Even from the document (Annexure 'H' of the writ petition) dated 7.3.83, the Ministry of Industries wrote to the Ministry of Defence for extension of lease period for 20 years. Thus, it is palpably clear that the Ministry of Industries in the Government of Bangladesh was taking all sincere efforts to extend the period of lease-hold interest of the appellant in the land after giving possession to the appellant. It is for the first time before the High Court Division, the Ministry of Industries in its Affidavit-in- opposition took the plea that, "it is stated that on the perusal of the documents annexed herewith and referred to above would reveal unambiguously that the respondent No.3 offered for sale only the plants and machineries of the undertaking known as Drum Metals Limited and for transfer of lease-hold interest in the land for the unexpired period of lease. Those documents further reveal and establish that the petitioner was clear in his mind that he was purchasing the plants and machineries and the lease-hold interest in the land for a limited period." 

 58. It may be mentioned that when the deed of agreement was executed, both the Government and the appellant knew that the factory was situated on the lease-hold land of the Government which was to expire in 31.3.83. Thereafter by (Annexure 'J' to the writ petition) extension was given by the Ministry of Defence Govt. of Bangladesh for 3 years up to 31.3.1986. Thus, the initial possession of the appellant on the basis of the agreement of sale was lawful and valid and during the continuance of the possession of the appellant the period of lease was further extended. Hence, it is clear that though the lease period of the abandoned factory expired on 31.3.83 the lease period was further extended during the continuance of the possession of the appellant. 

 59. The proposed sale between the appellant and the Government of Bangladesh was not a sale of two private individuals. But it is a sale between the Government on one hand and a private citizen on the other. This being a sale by the Government of a running Industrial concern and the Government as a policy decision having decided to disinvest the factory, the appellant came forward to purchase the same. In such a transaction, it will be the normal and reasonable expectation of a purchaser that he will be able to run the Industry after purchasing it from the Government. In such a situation the appellant was expected to take a reasonable view in the background of the case that when the Ministry of Industries of the Government of Bangladesh gave possession of the factory with the assurance that the lease-hold interest in the land would be extended for 20 years, the appellant reasonably put confidence in such a sale by the Government and invested his good money therein and went into possession. 

 60. Drums Metal Industries Ltd. by operation of law automatically and absolutely vested in the Government of Bangladesh. As per Article 4 of PO No. 16 of 1972 Government is the absolute owner of this Industrial undertaking having all the rights to administer, control, manage and dispose of by transfer or otherwise. Articles 4 and 5 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 authorise the Government after vesting of the property to administer, control, manage and dispose of the same. In pursuance of that statutory authority the agreement for sale was entered into and possession was delivered to the appellant. Hence, the possession of the appellant is that of a purchaser on the basis of an agreement. Whether the agreement will ultimately mature in the sale of the property, whether the right, title and interest in the lease-hold land will mature in favour of the appellant by virtue of a valid sale for a limited period is a matter to be determined on the performance of the agreement itself and that whether in future the seller (Government of Bangladesh), would lawfully transfer the interest or right in the land is a matter not within the scope of this proceeding, Hence, at this stage, I think that I amount to go into the ultimate question of the legal effect of agreement itself. I am only to see whether the possession of the appellant is that of a lessee as contemplated under section 2(c) of the Ordinance. The Government of Bangladesh being the vested owner by operation of law it cannot be said that the Government is a lessee or has acquired the interest of a lessee only and consequently, the appellant was also a lessee as inducted by the Government lessee. 

 61. From the admitted documents filed in this case, I find that the dispute was essentially an inter-ministerial dispute between the Ministry of Industries and the Ministry of Defence of the Government of Bangladesh. Both the Ministries having failed to arrive at a decision, ultimately most illegally took recourse to this manner of summary eviction under the cover of the Ordinance. The only question is of possessory right of the appellant and not the question of transferability of the right, title and interest on the basis of the agreement which may or may not mature into a full fledged sale at a subsequent point of time. 

 62. The learned Additional Attorney-General further submits that there being no bonafide dispute as to title of the Government, the Ordinance can be applied for evicting the appellant. On the other hand, Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed submits that title of the Government in the land is not at all disputed and the Ordinance cannot be confined only to the case of bona fide dispute as to title. The learned Advocate for the appellant and the learned Additional Attorney-General cited the decision reported in 20 DLR (SC)18, 20 DLR(SC)129 in support of their respective cases. 

 63. The case of Sufia Khatun as reported in 20 DLR (SC)18 relates to eviction of an unauthorised occupant under section 5 Act X of 1953. The case of Hatem Ali reported in 29 DLR(SC) 129 is also a case of section 5 relating to eviction of unauthorised occupant. In both the cases, it was held that the Act was designed to give power to the Government to take speedy steps for recovery of possession of Government land and in order to attain that purpose section 5 empowers the Government to make inquiry if a person is an unauthorised occupant on any land/building. In the case of Hatem Ali it was further observed that in such an enquiry the decision as to title by the Government shall not be final. Both the cases considered the case of possession of "unauthorised occupant" without the permission of the Government. It was in that context, under section 2(c) of Act X of 1953, the observation as to the bonafide dispute of title was made. But in the present case the appellant is not an unauthorised occupant and the reported decisions are not relevant in considering the case of purported eviction of a 'lessee' under section 3 of Ordinance No. LIV of 1965. The question of bonafide dispute as to title is irrelevant in the present case as there was no dispute of title, on the other hand, title of the Government is admitted. As a matter of fact, bonafide dispute as to title in the case of eviction of an unauthorised occupant under section 5 of Act X of 1953 is not the same thing of evicting outgoing lessee under section3 of Ordinance No. LIV of 1965, where title of the Government is in fact admitted by virtue of the lease. The question of bonafide dispute as to title is not relevant in the case of a lessee who is admittedly in possession by virtue of a lease from the admitted owner viz. the Government. Hence, the submission of the learned Additional Attorney-General cannot be accepted in the facts of the present case.
